title: Making the case
grammar: Formal suggestions and the subjunctive (I suggest that…, it's essential that…, it's important that he be…)

scene.speaker: nova
scene.bubble: Time to make your case! Learn to defend an opinion in writing and out loud — with a gapped-text read, formal suggestions, and the words that make an argument stick.
scene.intro: Welcome to Unit 5, B2. This term the Inspiring Nordic project needs more than good intentions — it needs a convincing case, on paper and out loud. In this unit you read a gapped-text feature in the format of Reading and Use of English Part 6 about how our reading club learned to argue well, you master formal suggestions and the subjunctive (it is essential that a case be proven, not just felt), you learn the linking words and so/such … that structures that hold a persuasive text together, and you write your first B2 First opinion essay. A good argument does not shout. It builds — paragraph by paragraph. Let's build one.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 1 and 2. Talk with a partner, then record yourself.

tips.expect: Part 1 (about 2 minutes): the examiner asks you and your partner questions about yourselves — opinions, free time, plans. Part 2 (about 4 minutes in total): each of you talks alone for about a minute about two of three photographs, answering the two questions printed above them; then your partner answers a short question about your photographs (about 30 seconds).
how: In Part 1, give reasons and an example, not one-word answers — but do not make a speech.
In Part 2, do not just describe the photographs. Compare them and answer the questions: speculate (they might be…, perhaps she's hoping to…) and give your view.
Keep talking for the full minute. If you finish one idea, move to the second question.
tips.remember: You are marked on your language, not on having the 'right' opinion. A clear, well-organised answer beats a long one.

data.text: Part 1: talk about opinions and persuasion. Part 2: compare two photographs and say why the people might be trying to persuade others.

parts.title: Interview
prompts: Do you enjoy giving your opinion in class discussions? Why or why not?
Tell me about a time you tried to persuade someone to change their mind.
Do you think it's important to listen to opinions you disagree with? Why?
Who is the most convincing speaker you know? What makes them convincing?

parts.title: Long turn
parts.question: Compare the two photographs and say why the people might be trying to persuade others and how they might feel about the reaction they get.

a group of people holding signs at a march

activities.title: Vocabulary — persuasion and argument. Match each word with its meaning.

pairs.right: a set of reasons put forward to support or oppose an idea
to make someone believe or do something by giving good reasons
a particular way of looking at or judging something
able to make someone believe that something is true or right
special importance or force given to a point
a personal view or judgement that is not necessarily a fact
facts or examples that support a claim
the final part of a piece of writing, where the main point is restated
to formally suggest an idea for other people to consider

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 6 — gapped text. Read the article and decide which paragraph fits each gap.

tips.expect: One text with six numbered gaps, followed by seven paragraphs (A–G) removed from the text and placed in a random order below it. One paragraph is extra and does not fit anywhere. You choose the paragraph that fits each gap.
how: Read the base text first, ignoring the gaps, to understand the overall argument.
For each gap, look closely at the sentences immediately before and after it: pronouns, linking words and repeated ideas point to the missing paragraph.
Check your answer by reading the gap and the paragraph together — the ideas must connect logically in both directions, not just one.
tips.remember: One paragraph does not belong anywhere. If a paragraph seems to fit two gaps equally well, look again: only one connection will be perfect in both directions.

data.title: Winning them over
data.text:
Every week the Inspiring Nordic team meets to plan how we will convince our school to invest more in the trades — carpentry, electronics, plumbing. It sounds simple: explain why it matters and people will agree. In practice, persuasion is a skill, and it can be learned like any other.

{1}

Our teacher, Miss Vega, calls this the difference between an opinion and a case. An opinion is what you believe. A case is what you can prove, paragraph by paragraph, to someone who does not yet agree with you.

{2}

Structure matters as much as passion. A reader — or a listener — needs to see where an argument is going almost from the first sentence, not guess at it by the final one.

{3}

Register matters too. Slang and exaggeration might work with friends around a table, but they weaken a formal case. Measured, careful language makes a writer sound like someone worth believing.

{4}

Perhaps the hardest habit to learn is dealing with the other side of the argument. Many students avoid it, worried that mentioning an opposing view will weaken their own.

{5}

Evidence is the final piece. A claim without evidence is just a louder opinion, and louder is not the same as more convincing.

{6}

None of this happens by accident. Every persuasive text we have studied this term — speeches, editorials, even adverts — follows some version of the same pattern: a clear thesis, an honest structure, a controlled register and evidence that does the talking. Master the pattern, and the passion can finally do its job.

paragraphs.text: The first step, Mateo discovered, is choosing a thesis and stating it early. “I used to bury my main point in the third paragraph,” he admits. “Now I put it in the first sentence, and everything else supports it.”

The opposite is true. Sofía argues that acknowledging a counter-argument, and then answering it, makes a writer look confident rather than uncertain. “If you ignore the strongest objection, your reader thinks of it anyway — and trusts you less because you avoided it.”

Liam, whose essays used to wander from point to point, now plans four paragraphs before he writes a single word: an introduction that states the thesis, two paragraphs that each defend one reason, and a conclusion that returns to the opening claim.

This is where facts, examples and expert opinions come in. Nadia keeps a notebook of statistics and quotations for exactly this purpose, so that when she writes that practical skills last a lifetime, she can immediately show why.

It also helps to remember your audience. A head teacher responds to different reasons than a group of classmates would, and a persuasive writer chooses arguments accordingly, without ever changing the main thesis.
This was Mateo's original assumption, before Miss Vega corrected him in front of the whole class, and he has never forgotten the distinction since.
Formal connectors — therefore, however, for this reason — signal exactly how one idea relates to the next, so the reader is never left guessing which way the argument is about to turn.

activities.title: Language focus 1 — formal suggestions and the subjunctive

data.title: Formal suggestions and the subjunctive
data.can: I can use the subjunctive after 'it is essential/important/vital that' and after 'suggest, recommend, propose' to sound formal and persuasive.
data.intro: To sound formal and persuasive — in an essay or in a speech — English uses the subjunctive: the base form of the verb, unchanged for any subject. Our reading text puts it simply: a case is 'what you can prove', and proving it often means writing 'it is essential that a paragraph have one idea', not 'has'.

examples.text: It is essential that every paragraph have one clear idea.
It is important that he be ready before the debate.
I suggest that she include a counter-argument.
We recommend that the school support the trades.
We recommend including real examples in every paragraph.
The head teacher proposed that a workshop open next term.

rules: After it is essential / important / vital / necessary that, use the base form of the verb: he be, she have, it stay.
After suggest, recommend, propose, insist, demand that, also use the base form: I suggest that he write (not 'writes').
The subjunctive does not change for the third person: he be, not 'he is'; she have, not 'she has'.
Recommend (and suggest) can also be followed by -ing, without 'that' or a subject: I recommend including an example.
This structure is formal register: use it in essays and debates, not in everyday conversation.

items.sentence: It is essential that everyone ___ on time.
I suggest that she ___ a stronger example.
It is important that he ___ ready before the debate.
It is vital that the register ___ formal throughout.
We recommend ___ a counter-argument in every essay.
The teacher proposed that the class ___ a debate club.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations

tips.expect: Six sentences. For each one you complete a second sentence with the same meaning as the first, using a given key word that must not be changed. You write between two and five words, including the key word. Each item is worth up to two marks.
how: Identify what is being tested — here, mostly the subjunctive and formal suggestions.
Write the whole gap, then read the complete second sentence: does it mean exactly the same? Is the key word unchanged?
Count your words. Contractions count as two words (didn't = did not).
tips.remember: Half marks exist: if the structure is right but a small word is wrong, you can still score one mark.

data.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first sentence, using the word given. Do not change the word given. You must use between two and five words, including the word given.

items.first: The teacher told the class to plan their essays first.
Students must include a counter-argument in their essay.
Sofía advised us to state our thesis in the first sentence.
items.second_end: our thesis in the first sentence.

items.first: It is very important for him to be on time for the debate.
Our teacher will not accept informal language in our essays.
His argument convinced everyone in the room.
items.second_end: that it convinced everyone in the room.

activities.title: Listening Part 2 — sentence completion. Complete the sentences with a word or short phrase.

tips.expect: A monologue lasting about three minutes — a talk, a podcast, a lecture. You complete eight sentences with a word or short phrase (never more than three words) that you hear. You hear the recording twice.
how: Before it starts, read the eight sentences and predict the kind of word that is missing: a noun? an adjective? a number?
The sentences follow the order of the recording. The words around the gap are often paraphrased, but the answer itself is the exact word or phrase you hear.
Write what you hear, spelt correctly. Do not change the form of the word.
tips.remember: If you miss one, let it go and follow the next sentence. You have a second listening.

data.voice_note: Presenter (short intro) + Miss Vega, English teacher, giving eight tips on writing and delivering a persuasive case.
data.script:
Presenter: On this week's episode for B2, Miss Vega joins us to talk about making your case — in a written essay and in a spoken argument. Miss Vega, over to you.
Miss Vega: Thank you. I want to share eight tips today, and I will take them one at a time. My first tip is about your thesis: decide your main point before you write a single sentence. Too many students discover their real argument in the last paragraph, when it is far too late.
Miss Vega: My second tip concerns structure. A convincing case does not wander; it moves in a straight line. I ask my students to plan four paragraphs: an introduction, two body paragraphs, and a conclusion that returns to the opening claim.
Miss Vega: My third tip is about register. This is written and spoken English for a formal situation, so slang and exaggeration have no place here. Choose careful, measured language, because that is what makes a reader trust you.
Miss Vega: My fourth tip, and one people forget, is the counter-argument. Always mention the other side, briefly, and then explain why your view is still stronger. It makes you sound fair, not weak.
Miss Vega: My fifth tip is about evidence. A fact, a statistic or a real example is worth more than three sentences of pure opinion, so keep a few ready before you start.
Miss Vega: My sixth tip is for the spoken version of your case — the debate, the presentation. Eye contact matters more than notes. If you are constantly reading from a page, your audience stops listening to your argument and starts watching your hands.
Miss Vega: My seventh tip: control your pace. Nerves make us speak too fast, and a fast case sounds like a nervous one, however good the content is.
Miss Vega: And my final tip: practise out loud at least twice before the real thing. Reading silently and speaking aloud use completely different muscles, and the exam rewards the second one. Good luck, and remember, a case is not a louder opinion — it is a structure that other people can follow.

activities.title: Language focus 2 — linking words for persuasion, and so/such … that

data.title: Linking words for persuasion, and so/such … that
data.can: I can use formal linking words (therefore, however, for this reason) and so/such … that structures to build a persuasive argument.
data.intro: A persuasive text does not just list ideas — it shows how they connect. Formal linking words like therefore, however and for this reason guide the reader from one point to the next, exactly as our reading text explains: 'Formal connectors … signal exactly how one idea relates to the next.' The structures so … that and such … that let you emphasise the effect of an idea.

examples.text: The evidence was so strong that nobody could disagree.
It was such a strong argument that even the head teacher agreed.
Practical skills last a lifetime. Therefore, schools should teach them.
Slang weakens a formal case; however, careful language builds trust.
The trades give real skills. For this reason, they deserve more time.
examples.note: for this reason = because of this

rules: Therefore, however, for this reason, as a result are formal linking words: use a full stop or semicolon before them, and usually a comma after.
So + adjective + that: emphasises the effect of a quality (so convincing that…).
Such + a/an + adjective + noun + that: the same meaning, but with a noun (such a strong argument that…).
Such + adjective + plural/uncountable noun + that (no article): such convincing evidence that…
Do not confuse so and such: so goes directly before an adjective; such goes before a noun (with or without an adjective).

practice.instructions: Choose the word or phrase that fits best.

items.sentence: The evidence was ___ strong that the panel was convinced.
It was ___ that everyone in the room agreed.
Practical skills matter to every student. ___, they should be part of the timetable.
Slang weakens a formal case; ___, careful language builds trust.
The trades give real skills. ___, they deserve more classroom time.
Her presentation was ___ that the head teacher asked for a copy.

activities.title: Reading and Use of English Part 1 — multiple-choice cloze. Choose the best word or phrase for each gap.

tips.expect: A text with eight gaps, each followed by four words or phrases (A–D) that are similar in meaning. You choose the one that fits the gap.
how: Read the whole text first for general meaning, without worrying about the gaps.
Look closely at the words before and after each gap: many options are near-synonyms, but only one forms a natural collocation or fixed phrase.
If two options seem possible, check whether one needs a different preposition or grammatical structure.
tips.remember: The four options are usually all real words with similar meanings — the difference is almost always collocation, not meaning.

data.instructions: For each gap, choose the answer (A, B, C or D) that fits best.
data.title: Winning the debate
data.text: Last month our class {1} a debate about whether schools should teach more practical skills. At first, I thought my opinion was enough, but Miss Vega soon changed my {2}. A good speaker, she said, does not simply state an opinion; she builds a {3}. That means choosing one clear idea and defending it with reasons an audience can {4}. I also learned that {5} matters: a debate is not the place for slang, however relaxed the room feels. Sofía's speech was the strongest example. She opened with a single sentence that {6} her whole argument, then gave two examples that made the case impossible to ignore. By the end, even students who had {7} with her at the start were nodding. What struck me most was her {8}: she never raised her voice, yet every word carried weight. I left the room wanting to write, and speak, exactly like that, and I have kept trying every week since.

activities.title: Writing Part 1 — essay. Plan, write 140–190 words and hand it in.

tips.expect: Part 1 is compulsory. You read a short question with three notes giving possible points. You write an essay discussing two of the three points and say which is more effective, giving reasons. 140–190 words, formal or neutral register.
how: Choose the two points you can say most about. Ignore the third completely.
Plan four paragraphs: introduction (the issue, no opinion yet) · point 1 · point 2 · conclusion with your decision and why.
You may use the opinions in the notes, but in your own words — copying them costs marks.
Link your ideas with linking words from this unit: however, therefore, for this reason.
tips.remember: The examiner marks content, communicative achievement, organisation and language. An essay that discusses three points, or none in depth, loses content marks however good the English.

data.task:
Your class has discussed what makes people change their minds about a cause. You have made the notes below.

Ways to persuade people to support a cause:

  • personal stories
  • statistics and facts
  • celebrities and influencers

Some opinions expressed in the discussion:

  • “A single story about one person can move people more than pages of numbers.”
  • “People trust numbers because you cannot argue with facts.”
  • “If someone famous supports something, people listen — whether they should or not.”

Write an essay discussing two of the ways in your notes. You should explain which way is more effective, giving reasons in support of your answer.

You may, if you wish, make use of the opinions expressed in the discussion, but you should use your own words as far as possible. Write 140–190 words.
plan: Introduction (1–2 sentences): introduce the question and name the two ways you will discuss. No opinion yet.
Paragraph 2 — first way: explain how it persuades people, with one example.
Paragraph 3 — second way: the same depth, using a linking word from this unit (however, for this reason).
Conclusion: say which way is more effective and why.

Developing a point: One clear example of this is…
Concluding: For this reason, it seems to me that…
Therefore, … is the more convincing way.

checklist: I have discussed exactly two of the three ways, each in its own paragraph.
My conclusion clearly says which way is more effective and why.
I have not copied the opinions word for word.
The register is formal or neutral: no contractions, no slang.
I have used at least one formal linking word and one subjunctive structure from this unit.
data.model:
A model answer (166 words).

Nowadays, charities and campaigns compete constantly for our attention, so knowing what persuades people to act is more useful than ever. Two of the most powerful ways are personal stories and statistics.

A personal story works because it turns a cause into a real person with a name and a face. When we hear about one child, one family or one street, we feel something that a chart cannot always produce. For this reason, most successful campaigns begin with a story, not a number.

Statistics, however, add proof once the feeling is there. A single fact — “one in five children” — can turn sympathy into a clear sense that the problem is serious and widespread, not just one sad case.

In my opinion, stories are the more effective way to persuade, because it is essential that people feel something before they act on the facts. Numbers convince the mind; a story convinces the heart, and it is the heart that reaches for a phone or a wallet.

activities.title: Speaking — Parts 3 and 4. Collaborative task and discussion. Record your best answer.

tips.expect: Part 3 (about 3 minutes): you and your partner discuss a question with five written prompts for about two minutes, then have about a minute to reach a decision. Part 4 (about 4 minutes): the examiner asks you both wider questions on the same theme.
how: In Part 3 you are not marked on agreeing; you are marked on interacting. Ask your partner's opinion, respond to it, build on it, disagree politely.
Do not try to cover all five prompts. Two or three in depth is better than five in a hurry.
In the decision minute, negotiate: Shall we go for…? I'd be happy with that, as long as…
In Part 4, develop your answers: opinion → reason → example → so what.
tips.remember: Look at your partner, not at the examiner. The examiner is listening, not talking.

data.text: Part 3: discuss how these things can make an argument more persuasive and decide which matters most. Part 4: discuss persuasion, opinions and how people are convinced.

parts.title: Collaborative task
parts.intro: Here are some things that can help someone win an argument. Talk to each other about how each of these might make an argument more persuasive.
parts.centre: How might these make an argument more persuasive?

parts.title: Further discussion
prompts: Do you think it's easier to persuade someone in person or online? Why?
Should schools teach students how to construct a formal argument?
Is it ever acceptable to use emotion, rather than facts, to persuade someone?
Who is more responsible for checking facts — the person persuading, or the person being persuaded?
Do you think people are becoming better or worse at listening to opinions they disagree with?

Involving your partner: Would you go along with that?
That's true up to a point, although…
Building on an idea: Following on from what you said…
Reaching a decision: I'd be inclined to go for…, on the grounds that…
We could agree to differ, but if we had to choose…
Part 4: developing an answer: There's a strong case for saying…

homework.prompt: Write a short paragraph (8–10 sentences) giving your opinion on a debatable topic of your choice — school rules, social media, or the environment. Use at least two formal suggestion/subjunctive structures (e.g. 'It is essential that…' / 'I recommend that…') and two linking words from this unit (therefore, however, for this reason, so … that / such … that).
